## Part 2: Multicollinearity, post-treatment bias, collider bias

- Show examples of each and how they can confound interpretations
- Show how models where causal interpretation is messed up can still do an OK job at predictions

### Multicollinearity 

```{r}
set.seed(1)
n <- 500

temp <- rnorm(n)
sun  <- temp + rnorm(n, sd = 0.3)   # highly correlated

growth <- 2*temp + 2*sun + rnorm(n)

dat <- data.frame(temp, sun, growth)
```


```{r}
m1 <- lm(growth ~ temp, data = dat)
m2 <- lm(growth ~ sun, data = dat)
m3 <- lm(growth ~ temp + sun, data = dat)
```

### Post-treatment bias

```{r}
set.seed(2)
n <- 500

fertilizer <- rnorm(n)

plant_size <- 2*fertilizer + rnorm(n)

fruit <- 1.5*fertilizer + 2*plant_size + rnorm(n)

dat <- data.frame(fertilizer, plant_size, fruit)
```

```{r}
m1 <- lm(fruit ~ fertilizer, data = dat)
m2 <- lm(fruit ~ fertilizer + plant_size, data = dat)
```

### Collider bias

Conditioning on colliders means you are creating an association between two variables that is not necessarily causal. Learning about the price of a bottle of wine inherently tells you something about its quality, but not because higher-priced bottles are necessarily higher quality. Instead, a bottle must be either high-quality or high-priced in order to achieve high acclaim. This means that if a bottle is priced low, it must be high quality, and vice-versa.

Unfortunately, when you decide to "control" for price in your model to test the impact of quality on acclaim, you are inadvertently testing for this non-causal association between quality and price, which leads to the conclusion that price increases quality, even though there is actually no relationship between the two.

```{r}
set.seed(3)
n <- 5000

gpa <- rnorm(n)
athletic <- rnorm(n)

admission <- gpa + athletic + rnorm(n)

dat <- data.frame(gpa, athletic, admission)
```

```{r}
cor(dat$gpa, dat$athletic)
selected <- dat[dat$admission > 1, ]

cor(selected$gpa, selected$athletic)
```

```{r}
set.seed(4)
n <- 500

temp <- rnorm(n)

predators <- 2*temp + rnorm(n)

prey_death <- 1.5*predators + 2*temp + rnorm(n)

dat <- data.frame(predators, prey_death, temp)
```

```{r}
m1 <- lm(prey_death ~ predators, data = dat)
m2 <- lm(prey_death ~ predators + temp, data = dat)
```

## Part 3: Overfitting

- Show when too many variables can explain more variation but make poor predictions

This will be a simulation we run together, and I talk it through with them. We will use a different number of predictors to see how bad the overfitting gets when we add too many random variables

```{r}
set.seed(10)

n <- 200

x <- rnorm(n, 5, 1)

# true relationship
y <- 2*x + rnorm(n, 0, 1)

dat <- data.frame(
  y,
  x
)

for(i in 1:80){
  dat[[paste0("z",i)]] <- rnorm(n, 5, 1)
}

# Training and testing data 
train_id <- sample(1:n, n/2)

train <- dat[train_id, ]
test  <- dat[-train_id, ]

# Simple model
m_simple <- lm(y ~ x, data = train)
summary(m_simple)

# Prediction error (training)
pred_train_simple <- predict(m_simple, train)
mean((train$y - pred_train_simple)^2)

# Prediction error (testing)
pred_test_simple <- predict(m_simple, test)
mean((test$y - pred_test_simple)^2)

# Overfit model
m_overfit <- lm(y ~ .,
                data = train)
summary(m_overfit)

# Training error
pred_train_overfit <- predict(m_overfit, train)
mean((train$y - pred_train_overfit)^2)

# Testing error
pred_test_overfit <- predict(m_overfit, test)
mean((test$y - pred_test_overfit)^2)

# Plot the predicted relationship between the simple model and the overfit model

# Simple model
plot(train$y ~ train$x)
lines(pred_train_simple ~ train$x)

# Overfit model
plot(train$y ~ train$x)
lines(pred_train_overfit ~ train$x)
```
